comparisons.peer_topic: Embedded segment net revenue and drivers for fiscal year 2024
comparisons.peer_summary: Embedded net revenue decreased by 33% to $3.6 billion in 2024 from $5.3 billion in 2023, primarily due to lower demand as customers normalized inventory levels.
comparisons.comparison: Both NVDA and AMD discuss the normalization of channel inventory levels as a key driver or context for their respective segment revenues in fiscal 2024. NVDA reports that its Gaming revenue increased 15% specifically due to 'higher sell-in to partners following the normalization of channel inventory levels,' indicating a recovery phase. In contrast, AMD reports that its Embedded segment net revenue decreased by 33% primarily because 'lower demand' persisted as 'customers continued to normalize their inventory levels,' indicating that the normalization process resulted in reduced shipments for AMD during this period. The core similarity is the explicit link between inventory normalization and revenue dynamics; the difference is the outcome: NVDA saw positive volume growth (sell-in increase) post-normalization, while AMD saw significant revenue decline due to lower demand during the continued normalization.

sentences.text: The increase reflects higher sell-in to partners following the normalization of channel inventory levels and growing demand.
The decrease in net revenue was primarily due to lower demand as customers continued to normalize their inventory levels.

peer_results.rationale: The supplied candidates (avgo_2024_7_D043, avgo_2024_7_D003) focus on the fiscal year calendar structure (52 vs 53 weeks) and its general accounting impact, not on specific business drivers, segment performance, or inventory dynamics comparable to NVDA's Gaming segment revenue analysis.

While Intc_2024_7_D036 mentions inventory normalization, it is in the context of the Client Computing Group (CCG) and compares 2024 metrics to 2022 as a base year, whereas NVDA compares 2024 to 2023. More importantly, the Intc candidate focuses on volume/ASP drivers for Notebooks/Desktops rather than the specific channel inventory normalization narrative driving Gaming revenue recovery seen in NVDA. The other Intc candidate (DCAI costs) is unrelated to the topic. A direct comparison of the specific Gaming/Channel inventory dynamic is not sufficiently aligned.

The supplied candidates (mu_2024_7_D009, mu_2024_7_D020) focus on inventory write-down mechanics (NRV) and R&D expense drivers. While mu_2024_7_D009 discusses inventory charges, it focuses on accounting impacts of write-downs from prior periods rather than the operational driver of channel inventory normalization affecting current sell-in volumes comparable to NVDA's disclosure.

comparisons.peer_summary: QCT revenues in fiscal 2024 increased primarily due to higher handset revenues driven by $2.8 billion in higher chipset shipments from major OEMs and higher automotive revenues from new vehicle launches with Snapdragon products, partially offset by lower IoT revenues; QCT EBT as a percentage of revenues increased primarily due to these higher revenues.

NVDA states that Gaming revenue increased 15% due to 'higher sell-in to partners following the normalization of channel inventory levels.' Similarly, QCOM attributes a $2.8 billion increase in handset revenues to 'normalization of customer inventory levels, which were elevated in the prior year.'
